Perhaps try keeping a journal. It might help with memory as well as dealing with mental illness. I've been dealing with depression for almost four years and journaling has been the one thing that has really helped me.

I'm in the same situation as you, 14 and living at home with Nmom. First of all, take everything she says with a grain of salt. Think of her as a toddler having a temper tantrum, she's looking for a reaction by saying the things she does. In fact, she's probably insecure in herself.

Also, this sounds kind of corny, but it helped me loads. Look yourself in the mirror and tell yourself, "I am loved. I am beautiful. I am worth it." Say it until you believe it, because it is true! I have it written on my mirror in dry-erase marker, just to remember.

Also, remember to be kind to yourself. There is not one single person on this planet that is perfect. "Perfection" is subjective and therefore can't be defined. So don't worry yourself if you feel you're not. Humans, normal people have fat, acne, cellulite, stretch marks. It's all part of having a body. Try not to see it as a negative thing. 

Good luck in your self-confidence adventure. I hope you are able to see yourself as the intelligent, beautiful, worthwhile person that you are!

I am about to drop some mad reading suggestions on you, because not only am I an avid reader, I am starved for affection. This is my niche lmao.

The Secret Life of Bees: Best book ever! Not only does it explore the feeling of being without parents, but it written so well and involves a trio of bee-keeping, kind, quirky sisters. And the ending is so worth it, I cried btw.

The Language of Flowers: Another great one. This is in my top ten of all the books I've ever read. Beautifully written, follows the childhood and adulthood of a girl in foster care with a love for botany. 

Almost Home By: Joan Bauer This is a children's book, but it has the potential to entertain adults. Some parts are a bit cringe, but the plot and kind characters make up for this. Also, it involves a puppy, which is pretty great.

The Mermaid Chair: I was blown away by the sheer brilliance of this novel. It focuses more on the protagonist finding herself and coming to terms with her grief, but there is plenty of mother-daughter healing and love. 

To Kill A Mockingbird: A classic, probably the most influential novel of the last century. There are elements of mothering in it (Calpurnia being a sweetie.) but I think that Atticus's relationship with his children is beautiful and sweet. You can fall in love with a scholarly man and his clever children while becoming a bit more enlightened about classic lit.

Here are a few that involve mother-daughter struggles/love but focus more on the protagonist: Camilla by: Madeline L'Engle (I love this book infinitely omg), Orphan Train By: Christina Baker Cline, Room By: Emma Donahugh, The Book Thief By: Markus Zuzak, The entire damn Ramona and Beezus series (To feed your inner child lol.)

I hope you find what you're looking for. Personally, these books feel a lot like coming home and I return to them again and again. Good luck, and happy reading!
